en: The Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Sole Realization of the Self-Vowed Samādhi, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Kuntimī, staying amidst the groves of a great forest.
In the Lushesha Vihāra, the site where he dwelt was named the Samādhi of Solitary Realization and Self-Vow.

At the beginning, when he first attained Buddhahood, the radiance was exceedingly bright, and there spontaneously appeared a numinous and auspicious precious lotus throne. Its flowers were fragrant and their brilliance permeated the ten directions; each flower had a thousand petals, and upon every petal sat a manifested Bodhisattva, attending him with dignified grace while suspended in the void. Each, from their respective positions, prostrated themselves fully on the ground, circumambulated him a thousand times, and then stood reverently before him. Together they raised their voices in a great sound, exclaiming in praise of this unprecedented marvel: "So be it, World-Honored One!"

We ourselves, in our own original lands, have seen the appearance of miraculous and auspicious trees. When these trees first sprout, their light illuminates Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The trees emit a profound sound; its tone is pure, plaintive, elegant, compassionate, and harmonious, penetrating deeply into the hearts of all beings. Those who hear it leap for joy, becoming fully endowed with equanimity and giving rise to the practices of the Mahāyāna. They perfect the six pāramitās and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, fully accomplishing all the works of a Buddha.

At that time, from each of the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Tathāgata dispatched a bodhisattva to proclaim the Way of the Buddha and illuminate the Mahāyāna, addressing those bodhisattvas:

"From this Buddha-land, you must travel across two more worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. There is a buddha-field named Sahā—'Sahā' meaning 'Endurance' in the language of Han—where the Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, One Who Has Transcended the Four Paths and Does Not Accept [Further Existence], Equal Enlightenment. He performs the work of a Buddha through the Dharma, the Vinaya, supernormal powers, and the teachings of the Buddha."
Each Tathāgata held a thousand-petaled lotus flower in his hand, bestowed it upon the Bodhisattva, and addressed him, saying: "Bear our names and pay infinite homage.

We rejoice that you, a true sage, have accomplished your merit and fulfilled your resolve, and that your realization of the Way is complete. You have descended your spirit into the five turbidities to shoulder the heavy responsibility for the masses; you have leaped over the ranks and stages to stand before Maitreya. With the great compassion of the six perfections, you universally rescue all living beings; may your daily life be free from ailment and your propagation of the Dharma ever victorious."
"Now that we have brought these flowers to constitute this Dharma-offering, we pray that all beings may universally assemble at this site of enlightenment.

Responding to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, those bodhisattvas suddenly vanished from their respective lands; they entered into a state of profound stillness and meditative concentration, and in a mere moment, they all arrived in the Sahā world.

Each rose from their seat and stood upright with dignified decorum, reverently honoring the Sage’s transformation by prostrating themselves on the ground. They then withdrew to circumambulate him seven times before returning to their original positions. With their supernormal powers abiding in the profound and their deportment solemn and majestic, their Dharma robes perfectly aligned, they raised their voices in unison and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Our World-Honored One, the Tathāgatas of our native lands send immeasurable greetings. We rejoice that you have fulfilled your merit and realized your vow, being fully endowed with the essence of the Way. You descended your spirit into the five turbidities to shoulder the heavy responsibility for the masses; surpassing others in rank, you stand before Maitreya. Through the great compassion of the six perfections, you universally rescue all living beings; your health and well-being are as excellent as ever, and your teaching of the Way is more sublime than usual.”
"I now present these flowers as a Dharma-offering, wishing that all beings may universally assemble at this site of enlightenment.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, O Righteous One!"

With joy, I receive the teachings of wisdom from those Tathāgatas; the samādhi of tireless perseverance flows forth unimpeded, and the dharmakāya—empty, pure, and luminous with wisdom—is fully perfected, such that this and that are of one essence.
I respectfully admire what I have heard, and my radiant joy is immeasurable.

At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni accepted these flowers with his own hands and smiled joyfully. Light issued from his mouth, universally illuminating the immeasurable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. He then scattered these flowers equally over those immeasurable Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
and those immeasurable Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, likewise caused their radiance to penetrate and pervade the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Every single sentient being, having received the Buddha’s compassionate light, attained the wisdom of contemplation and realized their past lives.

They illuminated one another in succession, shining down upon the hells; those in the three evil realms, the eight difficult conditions, as well as those in the heavens and among humans, all received this compassionate light and attained liberation. Hundreds of thousands of sentient beings became of one mind, universally resolving to seek the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
That light immediately returned, circled his body three times, and vanished into the crown of his head.

At that time, all the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were able to see one another through their mutual spiritual power; they universally enabled sentient beings to behold the Buddhas, for the manifestation of transformations ultimately remains as vast and empty as the eternal state.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Xianru (Wise Scholar), who immediately praised the Buddha in verse before him:
"How wondrous is the Great Sage’s transformation! Out of compassion for all living beings, For incalculable eons, He has accumulated merit and perfected his virtuous conduct."
Each and every meritorious deed, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, constitutes a single mark through a hundred blessings;
I pray to pay homage to the Honored One of the Three Realms.
How wondrous is the Great Sage’s transformation—his compassion and wisdom are boundless!
The Daoist path is pure and noble; the Buddhist Master is the God among Gods.
His great wisdom is supreme and unsurpassed; his Dharma-boat ferries all living beings.
His holy insight is pure and immeasurable; I pray to pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
How wondrous is the transformation of the Great Sage! His compassionate light moistens beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
The darkness of ignorance is forever removed, As are the distinctions between delusion and awakening, and turbidity and clarity.
His gracious benefits accord with the needs of the times, And his skillful means embrace all the common people.
"The Dharma-bridge delivers all beings; I vow to pay homage to the Honored One of the Three Realms.
Thereupon, the Holy Master said to the worthy scholar, "There are three causes and conditions for the smile of the Buddhas."
What are these three?

The wisdom of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is profound, far-reaching, subtle, and wondrous; it illuminates the three periods of time and penetrates the origin of sentient beings. As for those who proceed toward the three vehicles, each is fully endowed with their own fundamental practices, faculties, and faith.

There may be bodhisattvas whose resolve lies in their great vows; donning the armor of great virtue for the heavy responsibility of the masses, they sever the paths of worldly pursuit to serve as bridges for the world. They single-mindedly cultivate the six perfections without abandoning anything, dwelling steadily on the Path with ever-increasing courage and diligent effort. Their giving is free from conceptualization; their precepts, patience, and protective conduct are maintained; their meditative concentration is undisturbed; and their wisdom is clear and bright as they advance toward non-retrogression.
The Buddha’s eye perceives all such worthy sages and bestows a prediction of enlightenment upon each one.
It is not only a single Buddha who bestows this prediction upon them; all the Buddhas currently residing throughout the ten directions likewise bestow this prediction.
This is one cause and condition.
Furthermore, O worthy scholar!

If there is a bodhisattva who is directed toward the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), who has accumulated the roots of virtue and is fully endowed with noble wisdom, and who makes offerings to immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, receiving a prediction of enlightenment from each one; and who, through each successive prediction, clarifies and purifies Buddha-lands, universally moistening all sentient beings so that they share in a single practice.

He summoned the Buddhas, worthies, sages, and Great Benevolent Ones, serving as a great Dharma-ship across the four swift currents. He exhausted the ocean of the six desires and dried up the twelve gates; he entered the five paths and purified the five eyes. Concentrating his spirit in profound stillness, he dwelt in the Tuṣita Palace, gathering all bodhisattvas, realized beings, and upright men to purify their conduct within the three realms and preach the wheel of non-retrogression.
The Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions all join in praising such Bodhisattvas before the eight classes of beings, extolling their virtues and saying:
"Before long, they shall descend as spirits to become Buddhas, and all sentient beings throughout the ten directions will universally attain liberation."
"These are the two causes and conditions.
Furthermore, worthy scholars!

If there is a bodhisattva who, having completed his lifespan in the Tuṣita heaven, is about to descend and manifest in the world, he shall immediately enter the samādhi of ultimate and universal manifestation."

The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens universally surveyed the trichiliocosm, observing which kingdoms and cities were spacious and where sentient beings were gentle and harmonious; among the kṣatriyas, brahmins, elders, and householders in which cities and towns—out of those billions—were there those possessing the Way and virtue, who were pure, sincere, benevolent, kind, and wise?
The Wheel-Turning Sage King was currently residing in India, deliberating upon the descent of his spirit and the celestial beings who would serve as his retinue.

While appearing to dwell within the palace amidst maidservants and guards, he outwardly studied worldly affairs and contemplated the four marks of impermanence. A deva from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven exhorted him to leave the household life; he entered the mountains to refine his essence and sat beneath a peepal tree (*piṭala*). Shaving his hair and vowing to become a bhikṣu, he practiced the Dharma of the former Buddhas, taking the Dharma as his teacher and the Śuddhāvāsa devas as his witnesses. Within a single night, he attained the threefold transcendence, subdued the hosts of Māra’s officials, and fully accomplished the Buddha-work.

Trees of auspicious omens appeared throughout as many Buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges River; in each of those lands, every Tathāgata, amidst the eight classes of beings, praised the merits of the Bodhisattvas seated beneath those trees.
In this manner, each [Buddha] dispatched a bodhisattva from his own land to present flowers, pay homage, and extol the Mahāyāna.
Thus it is, O worthy scholar!
All the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions are fully aware of this; they joyfully celebrate as sentient beings gather universally at the site of enlightenment.
These are the three causes and conditions.

Those bodhisattvas who have come here are all those with whom the Tathāgata shared past causal connections; because he has preached the Dharma for them, they shall all attain the state of non-arising. Whether they are headed toward the stage of the Youthful (Kumārabhūta), or toward the stage of Birthlessness (Anupapatti), or toward the stage of Non-retrogression (Avaivartika), the Tathāgata has bestowed upon each of them a clear and complete prediction of their future enlightenment.
"You should know, O Noble One!
The Buddha does not smile without cause.
When these words were spoken, seventy billion nayutas of bodhisattvas attained the stage of the youthful (kumārabhūta).
Sixty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas attained the stage of birth;
thirty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas attained the state of *avaivartika*;
and one hundred thousand billion bhikṣus attained arhatship.
Nine hundred billion nayutas of people all attained the fruit of the path;
the devas of the three realms universally obtained the Dharma-eye.
Thereupon, the Holy Teacher spoke this verse:
“The Dharma-realm is entirely empty; the form-body is pure and true.
Dhāraṇī is the *pāramitā*; samādhi has no cause.
The Buddha-realm is likewise not empty; wisdom-purity is likewise not existent.”
"Compassionately regarding the world, you manifest a smile; O Righteous One, it is fitting that you accept [this teaching] swiftly.

Thereupon, among those in the assembly was the Bodhisattva Prabhādarśana, who immediately rose, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Holy Teacher from before him:
"I wish to ask a question."
"Only the Holy Teacher, with his immeasurable wisdom, has illuminated and explained what we had not heard before.
He replied, "Excellent!"
"Ask whatever you wish;
I shall now fully expound the essential points for you.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Light-Worthy Seen by the Eye.
“What is meant by a true person (satpuruṣa) who, having gone forth from home, fulfills the path, realizes it, and attains sarvajñā?
Thereupon, the Holy Teacher replied: “True person!
Listen well and pay close attention.
When the Buddhas leave the household life, they must first give rise to an aspiration, sitting upright to contemplate the profound stillness and penetrate the subtle mysteries.

When one focuses single-mindedly on mindfulness of the Way, there is inevitably a resonance; those who respond to this resonance are the gods of the Pure Abodes, Brahmā, and Maheśvara, who then command Śakra to manifest the four signs of impermanence—the images of old age, sickness, death, and suffering. Through these, he explains the realization of detachment from desire and the hardships of suffering, and the purity of mindfulness of the Way, so that one may dwell in mountains and marshes, refining one's essence and practicing dhyāna.

Just as this thought arose, the Four Heavenly Kings and their retinues arrived at the Peṭa tree; recollecting the manner of renunciation of former Buddhas, taking the Dharma as his teacher and the devas and Brahmās as witnesses, his root of faith was firmly established within. Having fully perfected the six perfections and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment through past habituation, he suddenly attained self-awakening regarding the Buddha-work. Thereupon, Śakra descended and placed a razor in his hand.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva grasped his hair with his left hand and held a sword in his right, thinking to himself:
"I shall reap the habitual stains of suffering and plant the root of non-attachment; I shall sever the flow of non-retrogression and enter the source of Nirvana."

"Since first generating the aspiration, they have always been able to leave the household life; their firm resolve is free from weariness, they are deeply non-regressive, they are fully endowed with faith and realization, and their mental intention is clear."
Before the blade had even reached his hair, it fell away of its own accord, and the *uṣṇīṣa* was naturally revealed.
The Bodhisattva, the successor to the seat of enlightenment, thought to himself:
"When previous Buddhas left the home life and shaved their hair, they should have possessed the dharma-garment of the *kāṣāya* to restrain the mind."
Just as this thought arose, the deva-son of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven immediately presented him with a naturally formed monastic robe made of pure, plain celestial silk.
Having accepted it, the Bodhisattva donned it upon his body; the dharma-garment was perfectly aligned and upright.

Thereupon, the Buddhas of immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all perceived one another through their mutual powers of manifestation; each sent a *kāṣāya* robe to bestow upon the Bodhisattva.

The Bodhisattva accepted them, and the Buddhas from both sides universally manifested their majestic spiritual power, causing all the robes sent by the Buddhas to merge into a single garment, which is named the *Sapīfotou Zhènyuè*.
This robe is now in the Brahma Heaven.
For this reason, I sat upright for six years to bring my past karmic conditions to an end; after those six years, at the end of the night, the realization of the precepts finally manifested.
What is meant by the "realization of the precepts"?

His resolve was set upon the seclusion of mountains and marshes to receive the Dharma; his spirit was true and his conduct far-reaching as he maintained the precepts and practiced the Way. He did not begrudge his life nor cast aside his body; he regarded all things with equanimity and sought no gain or sustenance. Guarding emptiness and practicing stillness, he constantly contemplated the pure Dharma; through the four immeasurables—compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity—and the fourfold kindness, he possessed unobstructed pity and clearly understood the four dhyānas. Free from flaw, free from defilement, and free from clever conceptualization, he did not follow the teachings of others, but within the Buddha-Dharma attained the path of Nirvāṇa.
"This is what constitutes a true śramaṇa of the precepts. The Buddha told them: "The pure precepts of a noble being (satpuruṣa) are formless and do not cling to the three realms.

They are without consciousness and without 'mine'; they are without self and without person; they are without life-force and without mind; they are without name and without lineage; they are without transformation and without number; they are without action. They come from nowhere and go nowhere; they are formless and without cessation; they are without body and without transgression; they are without mouth and without speech; they are without mind and without thought. They are without worldly affairs, without calculation, without activity, and without abiding. Furthermore, they are without precepts and without delusion; they are without mental objects and without decay. This is called the pure precepts."

The Buddha’s prohibitory precepts are without flaw or defilement, and there is no attachment to those who uphold them; they are free from anger and resentment, stable, tranquil, and pure. To follow the path that leads beyond the world in this manner constitutes upholding the precepts. Not receiving a physical form, not receiving a life span, and taking no pleasure in the five realms of existence—fully awakening others within the Buddha-dharma—this is what it means to uphold the precepts.
It is neither in the middle nor at the edge; it neither clings nor revolves, like the wind in empty space—this is the bodhisattva who maintains the precepts.

When the true person first sits beneath the tree, he purifies his initial observance of the precepts and realizes the truth; he abandons the root of suffering that is desire and relinquishes a distracted mind. His mind is free from the arising of thoughts: he has no thought of movement, no thought of pride, no thought of self, no thought of others, no thought of the middle, no thought of both self and others, no thought of the internal or external, no thought of the path, no thought of the mundane, and no thought of cessation.

He extinguishes the perception of non-existence, the perception of the absence of the perception of non-existence, the perception of the absence of the absence of the perception of non-existence, and the perception of the exhaustion of the inexhaustible.
Thus the True Man establishes his realization beneath the tree, purifying the eighteen hundred fundamental precepts.

When these numbers had concluded, the adamantine seat suddenly split open from the earth; the sixth celestial palace of Māra shook violently, and the various devas of the three realms were unsettled in their positions, all descending together to the Pippala tree to offer service and attend to him as was appropriate.
Suddenly, a great sound arose throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and within that great sound it was said:
"The Bodhisattva sitting beneath the tree shall realize enlightenment this very night.
All sentient beings heard and saw such a noble being.

This is the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the precepts, which brings about the realization of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), universally perfecting the three types of penetration, the six supernormal powers, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities, the ten powers, and the four fearlessnesses.

The three-thousandfold world system shook in six ways; the light of merit that subdues Māra shone everywhere, and sentient beings throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were graced by this compassionate radiance, attaining peace all at once and universally resolving to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, eight hundred bhikṣus attained arhatship;
thirty thousand devas and humans all attained the Dharma-eye;
and three thousand people attained the stage of anāgāmin.
When the worthy scholars and upright sages had attained the state of non-arising,
the Holy Teacher addressed the worthy scholars, saying:
"In the past, at one time, I traveled to the kingdom of Kuntimī."

At that time, the host of celestial Māras suddenly arrived with their retinues and entered the great assembly. Wearing strange garments, they mingled with the multitude, engaging in disputes and litigation, mutually slandering one another, and joining in discordant clamor. The bhikṣus, who were still subject to birth and death and unacquainted with the essence of the Way, became agitated with resentment and anger; each departed from the group and fled in different directions.
The Arhats and True Men each departed for the mountain forests.
At that time, O worthy scholar!

When the three months of summer had passed and the end of the year had arrived, it was the time for the *pravāraṇā*; on the fourteenth day, at night when the morning star appeared, he alone commanded Ānanda to strike the *gandī* and spread out the grass mats, so that he might observe the retreat together with Ānanda alone.
At that time, a devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens addressed the Buddha from mid-air:
"World-Honored One!
Now the assembly of bhikṣus has dispersed in various directions."
"Now that the Buddha has entered the retreat for the rains, why is he alone?
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"In the past, when I left the household life, you were my witness; when I went to the Bodhi tree, you again were my witness; now, as I enter the retreat for the rains, you once more are my witness."
Throughout the three thousandfold world system of Jambudvīpa, and across immeasurable worlds, the Tathāgatas have attained *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
From the moment they first attained Buddhahood until their entry into *nirvāṇa*, you have served as the third witness, fully endowed with the essential body.
You should know, O Devaputra!

Even the Tathāgata’s path-wisdom and supernormal powers, which walk alone throughout the triple world, must still be realized; how much more so for all ordinary beings who seek the Way—could they possibly do without a teacher?
He further addressed the Śuddhāvāsa devas:

"In the final age, many people will set their aspirations on purity; their resolve for the Way will be steadfast and clear, and they will take no pleasure in worldly affairs. They will dwell in seclusion within mountain forests, truly possessing a firm determination to leave the household life."

If you have no teachers or friends, you should follow the method of renunciation practiced by Mahākāśyapa: taking the distancing from desire as proof of its relinquishment; taking the distancing from the mundane as proof of its relinquishment; taking the distancing from fame and reputation as proof of their relinquishment; taking the distancing from physical form and the forgetting of form as proof of their relinquishment; and taking the distancing from seeking both internally and externally as proof of the relinquishment of seeking.
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!

By means of these five proofs, Mahākāśyapa shaved off his beard and hair, donned the kāṣāya, and took the Natural Dharma as his teacher. With pure resonance, he moved all the Buddhas of the ten directions, seeking their compassion and speaking thus:
'I look up with reverence to the devas of the triple world.'"

Having thus declared himself, these three proofs being clear and distinct, he immediately became a bhikṣu; he practiced the twelve dhūtas exclusively, each with firm resolve and without giving rise to thoughts of personal attainment.

"At that time, Kāśyapa attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) beneath the tree, and at the very end, he saw the Buddha and was immediately endowed with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Thus it is, O Devaputra!

Monks in the final age should contemplate this Dharma well; do not be arrogant, nor seek fame by disparaging the assembly in hopes of offerings. Nor should one, while falsely claiming to possess this Dharma, turn one's back on the community and refuse to take a teacher as a master."
This Dharma means that if there is no community of bhikṣus who can serve as teachers, one should aspire to practice this Dharma.

If there is a Saṃgha, one should seek the Saṃgha to act as witnesses. Because the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha—these Three Jewels—are equal to the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata (Tsa-to-lo-chieh) praises the community of bhikṣus who uphold the Vinaya as being supreme.
"You should know, O Son of Heaven!
Within the community of bhikṣus, there are ultimately three vehicles.
When these words were spoken, the Son of Heaven from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven and the assemblies of the eight classes of beings rejoiced upon hearing the sutra; they paid homage and departed.
The Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Sole Realization of the Samādhi of Self-Vow Spoken by the Buddha.
